questions.prompt: In the Linux kernel's own naming, which structure members are private per task rather than shared by the threads of a process?
options: The saved register/FPU state in `thread_struct` and the 16 KB kernel stack.
The `files_struct` descriptor table and the `fs_struct` cwd and umask.
The `sighand_struct` handler table and the `signal_struct` resource limits.
The `mm_struct` address space and the `nsproxy` namespace set.
questions.explanation: `task_struct` holds pointers to the shared resource structures, but the saved registers and the per-task kernel stack are embedded and private — that is exactly what makes a switch between two threads still a real context switch. The descriptor table is the most tempting wrong pick because it feels per-thread when you think about file positions, but `CLONE_FILES` shares one `files_struct` across the whole thread group, which is why one thread's `close()` is visible to all of them.

questions.prompt: A thread calls `getpid()` and `gettid()` and gets 4210 and 4217. What do those two numbers correspond to in kernel terminology?
options: 4210 is the kernel's TGID and 4217 is the kernel's `pid` field, the per-task ID.
4210 is the kernel's `pid` field and 4217 is the TGID assigned to the thread group.
4210 is the process group ID and 4217 is the session ID of the calling task.
4210 is the parent's TGID and 4217 is this task's own thread group identifier.
questions.explanation: The naming is inverted between POSIX and the kernel: what POSIX calls a PID is the kernel's `tgid`, and what POSIX calls a TID is the kernel's `pid`. So `getpid()` returning 4210 is the TGID shared by every thread, while `gettid()` returning 4217 is this task's own kernel `pid`. The swapped version is the standard confusion — it would imply threads each report a different `getpid()`, which is precisely the LinuxThreads defect NPTL fixed.

questions.prompt: `uptime` shows a load average of 40 on a 16-core box, yet `top` shows the CPUs mostly idle. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Many tasks are in `D` state, which counts toward load average without consuming CPU.
Many tasks are in `S` state, and interruptible sleepers are included in load average.
Many tasks are in `Z` state, and zombies keep accruing load until they are reaped.
Many tasks are in `T` state, and stopped tasks continue to be counted as runnable.
questions.explanation: Linux load average is the decayed count of tasks in `R` *plus* `D`, so uninterruptible sleepers — an NFS mount, a failing disk, a kernel-mutex convoy — inflate load with zero CPU use. Interruptible sleep is the tempting alternative but is deliberately excluded, otherwise every idle blocked server would show enormous load. Zombies and stopped tasks are not counted at all; a zombie holds only a `task_struct` and a PID.

questions.prompt: A process has been stuck in `D` state for ten minutes and `kill -9` does nothing. Why does `SIGKILL` fail to take effect?
options: Signal delivery requires the task to reach a signal check point, which an uninterruptible sleep never does.
`SIGKILL` is masked automatically while a task holds a kernel mutex, and the mask is cleared on wakeup.
The task has already been reaped, so the kernel has no `task_struct` left to deliver the signal to.
Uninterruptible tasks run at `SCHED_FIFO` priority 99, above the priority of the killing shell.
questions.explanation: `TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE` means exactly that the sleep will not be broken by pending signals; the check happens on the path back toward user mode, which the task never reaches. `SIGKILL` is not maskable at all, so the notion of an automatic mask is wrong even though it sounds like a plausible kernel protection. The diagnostic is `cat /proc/<pid>/stack` or `echo w > /proc/sysrq-trigger`, and the cause is usually storage or a stuck kernel lock that your process cannot recover from.

questions.prompt: A latency-sensitive process with 1 GiB resident in 4 KiB pages calls `fork()` once. What does the parent experience?
options: A 300 µs–2 ms stall for the page-table copy, then 1.5–3 µs COW faults on its own hot pages afterwards.
A 300 µs–2 ms stall for the page-table copy, after which the parent's mappings are untouched and run at full speed.
A near-constant-time call, because copy-on-write means no page tables are copied until a write occurs.
A 1.5–3 µs stall for the `mm_struct` allocation, with the whole 1 GiB copied lazily in the child only.
questions.explanation: The second-order cost is what people miss: `fork` marks writable private PTEs read-only in *both* processes, so the parent takes COW faults on its own working set after the call returns, landing the damage on the parent's critical path. The version that stops at the page-table copy is tempting because the stall figure is right, but it wrongly implies the parent is unaffected afterwards. And `fork` is O(mapped pages), not O(1) — COW avoids copying page *contents*, not page *tables*.

questions.prompt: Why does POSIX restrict a multithreaded program's child to async-signal-safe calls between `fork()` and `exec()`?
options: Only the calling thread is cloned, so any lock another thread held — notably the allocator's — is inherited locked forever.
The child's address space is shared with the parent until `exec`, so any write in the child corrupts the parent's heap.
Signal handlers are reset to default across `fork`, so a non-reentrant call in the child has no handler to recover it.
The child's descriptor table is copy-on-write, so any buffered I/O in the child races with the parent's file offset.
questions.explanation: `fork` clones only the caller; every other thread simply does not exist in the child, and whatever mutex they happened to hold at the instant of the call stays held with no owner to release it — a `malloc` call in the child then deadlocks. The shared-address-space answer describes `vfork`, not `fork`, which is why it reads plausibly. `pthread_atfork` is only a partial mitigation and the problem is widely considered unfixable in general.

questions.prompt: Which statement about what survives `execve()` is correct?
options: The signal mask and pending signals are preserved, while signal handlers are reset to their defaults.
Signal handlers are preserved, while the signal mask is reset to empty and pending signals are discarded.
Both handlers and the mask are preserved, since `exec` does not create a new process.
Both handlers and the mask are reset, since the entire address space is torn down and rebuilt.
questions.explanation: Handlers must be reset because the code implementing them is gone once the address space is replaced, but the mask and pending set live in the kernel and survive along with the PID, PPID, PGID and SID. Keeping handlers is the tempting answer because `exec` genuinely does not create a new process — but process identity surviving is a different thing from user-space code surviving. Ignored signals also stay ignored, since `SIG_IGN` needs no code.

questions.prompt: Your server opens a listening socket and then sets `FD_CLOEXEC` with `fcntl`. Occasionally a spawned child keeps the port alive after a restart. What is the defect?
options: The open and the flag-set are not atomic; a concurrent `fork`+`exec` in between leaks the descriptor.
`FD_CLOEXEC` set via `fcntl` applies only to the descriptor's file description, not to the descriptor itself.
`FD_CLOEXEC` is cleared by `execve` before descriptors are scanned, so it only works on the second `exec`.
Listening sockets are exempt from `FD_CLOEXEC`, so only `SO_REUSEPORT` can prevent a child inheriting them.
questions.explanation: This is a race window, not a semantic bug: between `socket()` returning and `fcntl(F_SETFD)` executing, another thread can fork and exec, and the child inherits a descriptor whose close-on-exec bit was not yet set. The fix is the atomic variant — `socket(SOCK_CLOEXEC)`, and likewise `open(O_CLOEXEC)`, `pipe2`, `accept4`, `epoll_create1`. The file-description answer is wrong in a subtle and appealing way: `FD_CLOEXEC` is genuinely a descriptor-level flag, which is why `dup` does not carry it over.

questions.prompt: A supervisor explicitly sets `SIGCHLD` to `SIG_IGN` and then calls `waitpid()` to collect a child's exit status. What happens?
options: The kernel auto-reaps children, so `waitpid` fails with `ECHILD` and no status is ever returned.
The kernel auto-reaps children, but `waitpid` still returns the buffered status of the last exiting child.
Children remain zombies because ignoring `SIGCHLD` only suppresses the notification, so `waitpid` succeeds.
`waitpid` blocks indefinitely because the ignored `SIGCHLD` cannot interrupt the wait to signal an exit.
questions.explanation: Explicitly setting `SIG_IGN` on `SIGCHLD` (like `SA_NOCLDWAIT`) tells the kernel to reap automatically, which means there is nothing left for `wait*` to collect and it reports `ECHILD`. The idea that ignoring merely suppresses the notification is the natural reading of "ignore" and is exactly wrong here — this is one of the few places where `SIG_IGN` has a semantic effect beyond discarding the signal. Auto-reaping and status collection are mutually exclusive: pick one.

questions.prompt: Why must a `SIGCHLD` handler call `waitpid(-1, nullptr, WNOHANG)` in a loop rather than once?
options: Standard signals do not queue, so several children exiting close together can coalesce into one delivery.
`waitpid` with `WNOHANG` reaps at most one zombie per second, so a loop is needed to drain the backlog.
The first `waitpid` call in a handler always returns `EINTR`, so at least one retry is mandatory.
Each loop iteration reaps one process group, and children may be spread across several groups.
questions.explanation: `SIGCHLD` is a standard (non-realtime) signal, so pending instances collapse to one bit: three children exiting while the handler runs produces a single delivery and two unreaped zombies unless the handler drains until `waitpid` returns zero or negative. The `EINTR` answer is plausible because handlers and `EINTR` genuinely interact, but `WNOHANG` makes the call non-blocking and there is nothing to interrupt. The handler must also save and restore `errno`.

questions.prompt: Which `clone()` flag combination produces the unusual middle ground of two tasks sharing memory but appearing as separate processes?
options: `CLONE_VM` without `CLONE_THREAD`, which is what `vfork` and some sandboxes use.
`CLONE_THREAD` without `CLONE_VM`, which gives one TGID over two address spaces.
`CLONE_SIGHAND` without `CLONE_FILES`, which shares handlers across distinct PIDs.
`CLONE_FS` without `CLONE_SETTLS`, which shares the working directory but not the TLS base.
questions.explanation: `CLONE_VM` shares the `mm_struct` while `CLONE_THREAD` is what joins the thread group and gives a common TGID, so setting the first without the second yields tasks that share memory yet are distinct "processes" to userspace — exactly the `vfork` and sandbox case. The inverted pairing is impossible in practice for a different reason than it looks: `CLONE_SIGHAND` requires `CLONE_VM`, and `CLONE_THREAD` requires `CLONE_SIGHAND`, so a thread group over separate address spaces cannot be constructed.

questions.prompt: How does `pthread_join` learn that the target thread has exited, without polling or signals?
options: `CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID` makes the kernel clear a TLS word on exit and issue a `FUTEX_WAKE` on it.
`CLONE_PARENT_SETTID` makes the exiting thread write its status into the joiner's stack and wake it.
The NPTL manager thread observes the exit and posts a condition variable the joiner waits on.
The kernel sends `SIGCHLD` to the thread group leader, whose handler releases the joining thread.
questions.explanation: `pthread_create` passes `CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID`, so on exit the kernel zeroes the registered word and performs a `FUTEX_WAKE` on that address — `join` is therefore just a futex wait, with no polling and no signal involvement. The manager-thread answer is a real mechanism, but it belongs to LinuxThreads, which NPTL specifically eliminated. Note also that `CLONE_THREAD` suppresses `SIGCHLD` to the parent entirely, so signal-based joining is not available.

questions.prompt: In the classic daemonization sequence, what does the *second* `fork` accomplish?
options: The final process is not a session leader, so it can never acquire a controlling terminal.
The final process becomes a session leader, so terminal signals are delivered to it directly.
The final process is placed in the foreground process group, so `SIGHUP` is no longer routed to it.
The final process is reparented to its own process group leader rather than to `init`.
questions.explanation: After `setsid()` the child *is* the session leader, and only a session leader can acquire a controlling terminal — so forking again and letting the leader exit permanently forecloses that possibility, and also orphans the daemon so `init` reaps it. Claiming the second fork makes it a session leader inverts the point: that is what `setsid()` already did, and it is the condition the second fork exists to undo. Under `systemd`, `Type=simple` services should skip all of this and stay in the foreground.

questions.prompt: Which kernel thread runs at `SCHED_FIFO` priority 99 and can therefore preempt an application RT thread at any priority you are advised to use?
options: `migration/N`, which handles stop-machine work, CPU hotplug and task migration.
`ksoftirqd/N`, which processes deferred softirqs when network load is high.
`kswapd0`, which performs page reclaim and can stall allocations for milliseconds.
`khugepaged`, which performs transparent-huge-page collection and compaction.
questions.explanation: `migration/N` sits in the stop scheduler class at FIFO 99 and preempts everything, which is exactly why the guidance is to place your own RT threads in the 40s–80s and stay below it. `ksoftirqd` is the most tempting alternative because it genuinely does preempt polling threads and is a real jitter source on NIC-heavy boxes — but it runs as an ordinary fair-class task, so it loses to any RT priority. `kswapd0` and `khugepaged` cause multi-millisecond stalls without any RT priority at all.

questions.prompt: What is the defining liability of an N:1 threading model compared with Linux's 1:1 model?
options: A single blocking syscall blocks every user thread, and the process cannot use more than one core.
Thread creation costs a full `clone`, so spawning is measured in microseconds rather than nanoseconds.
Each user thread needs its own kernel stack, so memory scales with the number of logical flows.
Switching requires a `CR3` reload, so every user-thread switch flushes translation entries.
questions.explanation: N:1 multiplexes many user threads onto one kernel task, so the userspace scheduler has no second task to run when the one it owns enters an uninterruptible syscall, and there is no way to occupy a second core. Expensive creation and per-thread kernel stacks are real properties, but of the 1:1 model — that inversion is the trap. A `CR3` reload never happens here at all, since every user thread lives in one address space.

questions.prompt: Why is an uncontended `pthread_mutex_t` lock roughly 15–25 ns under NPTL?
options: It is a `cmpxchg` on a user-space word; the `futex` syscall happens only when the lock is contended.
It is a `futex(FUTEX_WAIT)` syscall that the kernel short-circuits when no waiter is registered.
It is a spin loop bounded by the adaptive-mutex budget, which the kernel tunes per lock instance.
It is a vDSO call, which avoids the syscall trap while still executing the kernel's locking path.
questions.explanation: The futex design puts the lock word in user memory, so the uncontended acquire is a single atomic compare-exchange with no kernel transition at all; only when the compare fails does the thread pay ~2–8 µs for `FUTEX_WAIT`. The short-circuited-syscall answer is the most seductive because it also ends with "no wait" — but any syscall entry alone costs 40–350 ns, which already exceeds the quoted figure. Adaptive spinning exists in glibc but is a contended-case strategy, not the reason the fast path is cheap.

questions.prompt: A `thread_local` counter is fast in your executable but 5–20× slower when the same code is compiled into a `dlopen`ed shared library. Why?
options: The library uses the general-dynamic TLS model, so each access calls `__tls_get_addr` instead of a `%fs`-relative load.
The library's TLS block lives on the heap rather than in the static block, so each access takes a page fault.
`dlopen`ed libraries lose the `%fs` base register, so the runtime falls back to `pthread_getspecific`.
The library's TLS is protected by a per-thread mutex, so every access pays an uncontended lock acquire.
questions.explanation: Static TLS in the main executable resolves to a single `mov %fs:offset`, as cheap as a global, but a dynamically loaded module cannot know its offset at link time and must go through the general-dynamic model's `__tls_get_addr` helper. `-ftls-model=initial-exec` on hot libraries removes the call; `local-exec` is faster still but is valid only in the executable. The heap/page-fault answer is tempting because dynamic TLS blocks really are allocated lazily, but a fault would be a one-time cost, not a permanent per-access multiplier.

questions.prompt: You set `SCHED_FIFO` priority 50 in a `pthread_attr_t` and pass it to `pthread_create`, but the thread runs as `SCHED_OTHER`. What was omitted?
options: `pthread_attr_setinheritsched(&attr, PTHREAD_EXPLICIT_SCHED)`; the default inherits the creator's policy.
`pthread_attr_setscope(&attr, PTHREAD_SCOPE_SYSTEM)`; the default process scope ignores RT policies.
`pthread_attr_setdetachstate(&attr, PTHREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE)`; detached threads cannot hold RT policies.
`pthread_attr_setguardsize(&attr, 0)`; a nonzero guard size forces the thread onto the fair class.
questions.explanation: The default is `PTHREAD_INHERIT_SCHED`, so the policy and priority you carefully stored in the attribute object are silently discarded and the new thread copies the creator's — which is `SCHED_OTHER` unless the creator was already RT. This is the canonical "have you actually used this API" question. Scope is a real attribute, but Linux only supports `PTHREAD_SCOPE_SYSTEM` anyway; detach state and guard size have nothing to do with scheduling class.

questions.prompt: Which capability available through pthreads has no equivalent in the C++ standard threading and mutex types?
options: `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` on a mutex, the standard mitigation for priority inversion.
Timed acquisition of a mutex with an absolute deadline rather than a relative duration.
Waiting on a condition variable with a predicate that guards against spurious wakeups.
Shared-ownership locking where many readers may hold the lock concurrently.
questions.explanation: Priority inheritance is a mutex *attribute* in POSIX and `std::mutex` exposes no attribute surface at all, which is on its own a sufficient reason to drop to pthreads in a real-time process. Absolute-deadline acquisition looks like a gap but `std::timed_mutex::try_lock_until` provides it; predicate-form `wait` and `std::shared_mutex` cover the other two. Stack size, affinity and scheduling policy at creation time are the other genuine gaps in the C++ interface.

questions.prompt: A function declares `char buf[65536]` and writes to its first element. Why can this corrupt memory despite the thread having a guard page?
options: A single large stack adjustment can skip past the one-page guard and land in the mapping below it.
Guard pages are mapped read-only rather than `PROT_NONE`, so a write of under a page size succeeds silently.
Guard pages sit above the thread stack, and stacks grow downward away from the protected region.
Guard pages are installed only on the main thread's stack, so pthread stacks have no protection at all.
questions.explanation: The guard is one `PROT_NONE` page by default, and `sub $65536, %rsp` followed by a touch near the new top of frame can jump clean over it into whatever is mapped below, corrupting instead of faulting. `-fstack-clash-protection` makes the compiler probe each page as the frame extends, guaranteeing the guard is hit. The claim that the guard is above the stack inverts the layout — it is placed at the low end, which is where a downward-growing stack arrives.

questions.prompt: A service creates 1,000 threads at the default stack size. What is the actual resource impact?
options: About 8 GiB of virtual address space but only ~10 MiB of RSS, since stacks are demand-paged.
About 8 GiB of resident memory, since pthreads pre-faults each stack to avoid faults under load.
About 10 MiB of virtual address space, since glibc caches and shares freed stacks between threads.
About 8 GiB of both address space and resident memory, since `mmap` of a stack implies `MAP_POPULATE`.
questions.explanation: Each non-main stack is a fixed 8 MiB `mmap` region, but RSS grows only with pages actually touched — typically one or two pages, 4–12 KiB per thread. The real cost is address-space consumption plus a minor page fault of 0.5–2 µs on each new stack page's first touch, which is why a thread that first recurses deeply under load pays a burst of faults at the worst moment. glibc does cache freed stacks for reuse, but that reduces `mmap` calls, not the virtual footprint of live threads.

questions.prompt: What can a stackful fiber do that a C++20 coroutine cannot?
options: Suspend from inside a nested function call, because it owns a real stack that can be swapped out.
Resume on a different carrier thread, because its state is captured in an independent register set.
Switch in a few nanoseconds, because the transfer compiles down to an ordinary indirect call.
Avoid heap allocation entirely, because its state lives in registers rather than a separate frame.
questions.explanation: The stackful/stackless distinction is exactly this: a fiber swaps a whole stack so any depth of call chain can suspend, whereas a coroutine is a compiler-generated state machine that can only suspend from its own body. The switch-cost answer is a true statement about coroutines (~2–10 ns, often inlined away) attached to the wrong subject — fibers pay 20–100 ns for a register swap, so it is the coroutine that is faster. A fiber also does not avoid allocation; it needs a whole stack up front.

questions.prompt: A fiber running on a carrier thread issues a blocking `read()` on a socket. What happens to the other fibers scheduled on that carrier?
options: They stall until the syscall returns, because fibers are cooperative and the kernel blocks the whole task.
They continue, because the user-space scheduler receives a signal on entry to the syscall and reschedules.
They migrate to another carrier thread automatically, since fiber schedulers are work-stealing by design.
They continue, because a blocking syscall from a fiber is converted to a non-blocking one by the runtime.
questions.explanation: The kernel knows only about the carrier task; when it blocks, every fiber multiplexed onto it stops, and there is no timer interrupt that can preempt a fiber back into the scheduler because fiber switching is purely cooperative. This is why fiber runtimes must intercept every blocking operation. The auto-conversion answer describes what a mature runtime like Go's does *by wrapping the call sites*, not something that happens to a raw `read()` — the interception is the work, not a property of fibers.

questions.prompt: Which cost dominates the total impact of a context switch on a latency-sensitive thread?
options: Cache and branch-predictor pollution, at 10–100 µs of degraded execution afterwards.
The direct kernel work of saving state and picking the next task, at 1–3 µs.
The `CR3` reload with PCID enabled, at roughly 200 cycles per address-space change.
The FPU and AVX-512 state save and restore, at 100–300 cycles per switch.
questions.explanation: The kernel's own work is 1–3 µs, but the evicted L1/L2 and polluted branch predictors leave the thread running degraded for 10–100 µs after it resumes — an order of magnitude more, and invisible in any counter that only measures switch duration. The 1–3 µs figure is the tempting answer precisely because it is the number people measure. The `CR3` and XSAVE costs are real but are sub-microsecond contributions to the direct half.

questions.prompt: `perf stat` shows zero context switches for your pinned busy-poll thread, yet its cycles-per-instruction is far above what you measured on an idle box. What is the most likely cause?
options: A task on the SMT sibling is competing for the same L1, µop cache and execution ports.
The thread is taking involuntary switches that `perf stat` cannot attribute to a pinned task.
The RT throttle is descheduling the thread for 50 ms per second, which raises average CPI.
The thread is migrating between NUMA nodes, so its working set has become remote.
questions.explanation: SMT contention degrades you without ever taking the CPU away — the sibling hyperthread shares the physical core's front end and execution resources continuously, so the symptom is elevated CPI with a switch count of exactly zero. That signature is what rules out the alternatives: throttling and involuntary preemption both show up as context switches, and migration is impossible for a thread pinned to one CPU. The fixes are disabling SMT or isolating both siblings and leaving one idle.

questions.prompt: Under CFS, how is a task's `vruntime` related to its nice value?
options: `vruntime` advances in inverse proportion to weight, so a low-nice task accumulates it more slowly and is picked more often.
`vruntime` advances in direct proportion to weight, so a low-nice task accumulates it faster and is picked more often.
`vruntime` ignores weight entirely; nice values instead scale the timeslice granted once a task is selected.
`vruntime` advances at wall-clock rate for all tasks; nice values instead bias the red-black tree insertion point.
questions.explanation: The update is `vruntime += delta_exec × (NICE_0_WEIGHT / task_weight)`, so a heavier (lower-nice) task divides by a larger weight and its virtual clock runs slower — and since CFS always runs the smallest `vruntime`, it wins the tree more often. Each nice level is roughly a 1.25× weight change, about 10% of CPU. The direct-proportion version reaches the right conclusion by exactly inverted reasoning, which is the trap: if `vruntime` grew faster for a favoured task it would be selected *less*.

questions.prompt: A containerized service shows multi-millisecond tail latency spikes with no visible CPU saturation. Which diagnostic should you check first?
options: `cpu.stat`'s `nr_throttled` and `throttled_usec`, since `cpu.max` stalls the whole group until the period rolls over.
`cpu.weight`, since a low relative share starves the group whenever any sibling cgroup becomes runnable.
`sched_wakeup_granularity_ns`, since a waking task needs that much `vruntime` advantage to preempt.
`sched_migration_cost_ns`, since a task considered cache-hot is never migrated off a saturated CPU.
questions.explanation: `cpu.max` is a hard quota: once the group exhausts `quota` within a `period`, every task in it is stopped until the period rolls over, which is a multi-millisecond stall that looks like a GC pause and shows low average utilization — the single most common cause of mysterious container tail latency. `cpu.weight` is the tempting sibling knob, but it distributes *shares* proportionally and never stops a group when spare capacity exists. The scheduler tunables affect wakeup ordering, not periodic hard stalls.

questions.prompt: Two CPU-bound threads are both `SCHED_FIFO` at priority 60 and pinned to the same CPU. What happens?
options: The first to run holds the CPU until it blocks or yields, since FIFO has no timeslice among equals.
They alternate every 100 ms, since the `sched_rr_timeslice_ms` quantum applies to all RT policies.
They alternate every 0.75–3 ms, since the fair-class base slice still bounds any runnable task.
They alternate every 50 ms, since the RT throttle rotates equal-priority tasks within each period.
questions.explanation: `SCHED_FIFO` has no quantum at all: same-priority tasks run in FIFO order and the running one is displaced only by a strictly higher priority task, a block, or an explicit yield. Round-robin among equals with a 100 ms quantum is `SCHED_RR` — swapping the two policies' behaviour is the classic error this question targets. The RT throttle does interrupt them, but it forces time to *non-RT* work rather than rotating the two RT threads against each other.

questions.prompt: With default RT throttling, what does a busy-polling `SCHED_FIFO` thread experience?
options: A forced deschedule of roughly 50 ms once per second, since RT gets 950 ms of each 1 s period per CPU.
A forced deschedule of roughly 5 ms once per second, since RT gets 995 ms of each 1 s period per CPU.
A gradual priority decay toward 0 over each period, restored when the thread next blocks voluntarily.
No effect at all, since throttling applies only to `SCHED_RR` tasks that exhaust their round-robin quantum.
questions.explanation: `sched_rt_period_us` is 1,000,000 and `sched_rt_runtime_us` is 950,000, so RT tasks get 95% of each second per CPU and the remaining 5% — about 50 ms — is forcibly handed to non-RT work. The diagnostic signature is a *perfectly periodic* 1 Hz stall of tens of milliseconds, which people chase for days. The exemption answer is appealing because throttling and quanta both sound like time-slicing, but throttling is a class-wide budget that covers FIFO precisely because FIFO has no quantum of its own.

questions.prompt: Why is running an application thread at `SCHED_FIFO` priority 99 a bad idea?
options: It ties with the kernel's stop-machine and watchdog threads, so a spinning thread can wedge the machine.
It exceeds `RLIMIT_RTPRIO`'s hard maximum of 98, so `pthread_setschedparam` returns `EPERM` regardless.
It is silently demoted to `SCHED_RR`, because the kernel reserves policy 99 for `SCHED_DEADLINE` tasks.
It disables RT throttling for that task, so the thread never yields any time to housekeeping work.
questions.explanation: Priority 99 is where `migration/N` and the watchdog live, so an application thread that spins there can prevent stop-machine work and lockup detection from ever running and hang the box; the guidance is to pick something in the 40s–80s. The throttle answer is tempting because it correctly describes the *consequence* of a spinning RT thread, but the throttle is a global budget that applies at every RT priority — 99 does not exempt you from it, it just puts you above the kernel threads that would otherwise clean up after you.

questions.prompt: In `pick_next_task()`, which scheduling class is consulted before the others on each run queue?
options: The stop class, then deadline, then RT, then fair, then idle.
The deadline class, then stop, then RT, then fair, then idle.
The RT class, then deadline, then stop, then fair, then idle.
The fair class, then RT, then deadline, then stop, then idle.
questions.explanation: The order is strict and fixed: `stop_sched_class` (which is `migration/N`), then `dl_sched_class` for `SCHED_DEADLINE`, then `rt_sched_class` for FIFO and RR, then `fair_sched_class` for CFS/EEVDF, then idle. Putting deadline ahead of stop is the most plausible slip because `SCHED_DEADLINE` genuinely does outrank FIFO and RR — but nothing outranks stop-machine, which is the whole reason it exists as a separate class.

questions.prompt: Your producer and consumer threads are unpinned `SCHED_OTHER`, and you observe that they frequently end up on the same core. What mechanism is responsible?
options: `select_task_rq_fair`'s wake affinity, which prefers to place a waking task on a CPU sharing cache with its waker.
The load balancer's periodic domain rebalance, which consolidates tasks onto the fewest cores to save power.
`sched_wakeup_granularity_ns`, which forces a waking task onto the waker's run queue until it accrues lag.
The autogroup mechanism, which pins all tasks in one session to a single CPU to preserve cache locality.
questions.explanation: `wake_affine` deliberately trades run-queue depth against cache locality and places the wakee near the waker, which is usually right and occasionally piles a producer and consumer onto one core or bounces a thread across NUMA nodes. Pinning removes the heuristic from the equation entirely. Wakeup granularity is a real tunable but governs whether the wakee *preempts* the current task, not which CPU it lands on; autogroup groups tasks by session for weight purposes and does not pin anything.

questions.prompt: You call `sched_setaffinity(getpid(), sizeof(set), &set)` in a process with twelve threads. What is the effect?
options: Only the main thread is pinned, because the first argument is interpreted as a TID.
All twelve threads are pinned, because affinity is stored per thread group in the `signal_struct`.
The call fails with `EINVAL`, because a TGID is not a valid target for an affinity change.
All twelve threads are pinned, but new threads created afterwards revert to the full CPU mask.
questions.explanation: Affinity is a per-task bitmask and the syscall's first argument is a TID, so passing a TGID happens to name the main thread — whose TID equals the TGID — and silently pins that one thread only. `taskset -p` has the same failure mode. To cover a whole process you must iterate `/proc/<pid>/task/*`. The call does not fail, which is what makes this insidious: it succeeds and you believe you are pinned.

questions.prompt: A worker allocates and initializes its large ring buffer, then pins itself to a CPU on another NUMA node. What is the consequence?
options: The pages stay on the original node, so every access is remote at 1.4–2× latency until they are migrated.
The pages migrate with the thread on the next access, costing one minor fault per page and nothing further.
The pin fails with `EINVAL`, because a thread cannot move to a node holding none of its resident pages.
The pages are replicated onto the new node automatically, doubling the buffer's resident footprint.
questions.explanation: First-touch allocation binds each page to the node where it was first written, and nothing moves it afterwards just because the thread did — the working set becomes permanently remote at 1.4–2× access latency. The correct order is pin, then allocate and touch, then start work. Automatic migration on next access is the appealing wrong answer because Linux does have NUMA balancing, but it is a sampling heuristic operating over seconds, not a per-access guarantee you can design around.

questions.prompt: On a two-socket Intel box with interleaved CPU enumeration and SMT enabled, you pin two hot threads to CPU 0 and CPU N (where N is the core count). What have you done?
options: Placed both threads on the SMT siblings of one physical core, halving throughput while `top` shows two cores busy.
Placed the two threads on separate sockets, so every cache-line handoff between them crosses the interconnect.
Placed both threads on the same physical core but on separate L2 slices, which costs only a small L2 miss penalty.
Placed the two threads on separate physical cores of one socket, which is the recommended producer/consumer layout.
questions.explanation: Under interleaved enumeration the first N logical CPUs are one thread of every core and CPUs N..2N-1 are their siblings in the same order, so CPU 0 and CPU N are the two hyperthreads of one physical core — they share L1, L2, µop cache and execution ports, giving a 1.2–2× slowdown with no context switch to explain it. The cross-socket answer is a reasonable guess for a high-numbered CPU under *sequential* enumeration, which is why you must read `lscpu -e` or `thread_siblings_list` rather than assume either scheme.

questions.prompt: You boot with `nohz_full=2-7` but `perf stat -e irq_vectors:local_timer_entry -C 4` still reports about 1000 events per second. What is the most likely reason?
options: More than one task is runnable on CPU 4; tickless operation requires exactly one runnable task.
`nohz_full` suppresses only the 250 Hz accounting tick, so the 1000 Hz preemption tick remains.
`nohz_full` takes effect only when combined with `rcu_nocbs`, which was omitted from the boot line.
The counter reports the residual 1 Hz tick multiplied by the number of isolated CPUs in the mask.
questions.explanation: Tickless operation is conditional, not absolute: the moment a second task becomes runnable on that CPU — a stray kernel thread is enough — the tick returns at full rate, so the fix is to find what else landed there. `rcu_nocbs` is a genuine companion boot parameter and belongs on the line, but omitting it offloads nothing while still leaving `nohz_full` functional, so it does not explain a full-rate tick. The expected reading on a correctly isolated CPU is around 1/s, not 1000/s.

questions.prompt: Your core is fully isolated with `nohz_full`, `rcu_nocbs`, `irqaffinity` and `idle=poll`, yet you still see occasional 200 µs spikes. What remaining source should you investigate?
options: Firmware SMIs, which are invisible to the OS and detectable only via `hwlatdetect` or the SMI-count MSR.
CFS load balancing, which will still migrate a task onto an `isolcpus` CPU when other cores are saturated.
The RT throttle, which forcibly yields 5% of each second even on a CPU removed from the scheduler domains.
The `rcuo` offload kthreads, which `rcu_nocbs` relocates onto the isolated CPU that generated the callbacks.
questions.explanation: System Management Interrupts are taken by firmware below the operating system, can last 100 µs to 1 ms, and no kernel setting removes them — checking for them is the strong answer to "I isolated everything and still see spikes." The RT throttle is a real 50 ms-per-second hazard but produces a perfectly periodic 1 Hz stall of tens of milliseconds, not a sporadic 200 µs one, and `isolcpus` specifically removes the CPU from the balancer's domains. `rcu_nocbs` moves callbacks *off* the isolated CPU onto housekeeping cores.

questions.prompt: What is the failure mode of under-provisioning housekeeping CPUs on a heavily isolated box?
options: Kernel work backs up until the kernel schedules it onto an isolated core anyway, reintroducing the jitter.
Interrupts targeted at housekeeping CPUs are dropped once their queues fill, causing silent packet loss.
The kernel refuses to bring the isolated CPUs online at boot, so the isolation configuration never applies.
`irqbalance` re-enables itself to redistribute the backlog, overwriting the configured IRQ affinities.
questions.explanation: Isolation only relocates work; if the cores absorbing it are too few, `ksoftirqd` starts running, the backlog grows, and eventually the kernel places that work on an isolated core because nothing else can make progress — you get the jitter back, having done all the tuning. Two to four housekeeping cores on a 32-core box is typical. The `irqbalance` answer names a real hazard, but the daemon overwrites affinities whenever it is left enabled, not as a reaction to load; you disable it explicitly.

questions.prompt: Why is `sched_yield()` inside a spin loop an anti-pattern, particularly under `SCHED_FIFO`?
options: It is a 200–350 ns syscall and moves you to the tail of your priority's run queue, which can be worse than not yielding.
It drops the task to `SCHED_OTHER` for the remainder of the period, so it loses its real-time priority entirely.
It blocks until the next timer tick, so on a tickless CPU the yielding thread can stall for a full second.
It counts as a voluntary context switch against the RT throttle budget, exhausting the 950 ms allowance early.
questions.explanation: You pay a real syscall for the privilege of going to the back of the FIFO queue at your priority, letting every other same-priority task run first — the opposite of what a spinner wants. `_mm_pause()` is the correct instruction: it frees SMT execution resources, cuts power, and avoids the memory-ordering machine clear when the awaited value finally changes. The throttle answer is wrong on mechanism: the throttle accounts RT *runtime* consumed, and yielding does not spend budget faster.

questions.prompt: A hot path is audited as fully lock-free but occasionally shows a growing `voluntary_ctxt_switches` count. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A hidden blocking operation such as `malloc` taking an arena lock, a log write, or a first-touch page fault.
The RT throttle preempting the thread, which the kernel accounts as a voluntary switch by convention.
The 1000 Hz timer tick, which records a voluntary switch each time it re-selects the running task.
An SMT sibling contending for execution ports, which forces the thread to yield the core.
questions.explanation: A voluntary switch means the task blocked of its own accord, so on a supposedly lock-free path it is the signature of hidden blocking: `malloc` taking an arena lock or calling `mmap`, `std::cout` taking a locale lock and issuing `write`, a page touched for the first time, or a `std::vector` growing. Throttling is the tempting alternative because it does stall an RT thread — but being preempted by the kernel is recorded as an *involuntary* switch, which is the distinction the counter exists to draw. Detect with `perf trace` or `bpftrace` on `sys_enter` filtered to the hot thread.
